title: Shakespeare: The Great Word-Forger
description: The man who invented over 1,700 words and phrases that still shape how we speak today

photo.description: Portrait of a balding man with mustache and small pointed beard, wearing an elaborate white ruff collar, intelligent piercing eyes

questions.question: Name this playwright who invented words like 'assassination', 'swagger', and 'eyeball'
questions.hint: He wrote approximately 37 plays and 154 sonnets
questions.explanation: William Shakespeare (1564-1616) is credited with coining over 1,700 words and phrases that entered English permanently, from 'bedroom' to 'fashionable' to 'lonely'.
questions.wordInventor: The greatest linguistic innovator in English history

questions.question: Shakespeare invented the word 'assassination' for which play about a Roman leader's murder?
questions.hint: The play features the Ides of March warning
questions.explanation: Shakespeare coined 'assassination' in 'Julius Caesar' (1599). The word comes from the Arabic 'hashshashin' (hashish users), referring to medieval Muslim sect killers.
questions.etymologyCreation: From Arabic hashish-users to Shakespearean invention

questions.question: What common word meaning 'to kill' did Shakespeare first use in 'Macbeth', derived from a Middle English word for striking?
questions.hint: It's associated with the phrase 'things that go ___ in the night'
questions.explanation: Shakespeare first used 'bump' in its violent sense in 'Macbeth'. The word evolved from Middle English 'bumpen' (to strike) to our modern usage in 'bump off'.
questions.linguisticEvolution: How Shakespeare transformed everyday words into violence

questions.question: Shakespeare created the phrase 'green-eyed monster'. In which play does Iago use this phrase to describe jealousy?
questions.hint: The play features a Moorish general and his manipulative ensign
questions.explanation: In 'Othello', Iago warns: 'O, beware, my lord, of jealousy! It is the green-eyed monster which doth mock the meat it feeds on.' Shakespeare linked green eyes to envy permanently.
questions.colorPsychology: How Shakespeare embedded psychological insight into language

questions.question: What word meaning 'alone' did Shakespeare invent in 'Coriolanus', combining 'one' with 'like'?
questions.hint: Before Shakespeare, people said 'solitary' or 'alone' but not this emotional word
questions.explanation: Shakespeare created 'lonely' in 'Coriolanus' (1608) by combining 'lone' with '-ly'. Before this, English lacked a word for the emotional state of being alone.
questions.emotionalLanguage: Shakespeare invented the vocabulary of human feelings

deeperMode.title: The Shakespeare Authorship Laboratory
deeperMode.description: Forensic linguistics and the mysteries surrounding Shakespeare's identity and lost years

questions.question: Computational stylometry analysis shows Shakespeare's late plays have unusually high rates of what type of word, suggesting collaboration with younger writers?
questions.hint: These are grammatical words rather than content words
questions.explanation: Stylometric analysis reveals Shakespeare's late plays show different patterns in function word usage, suggesting collaboration with John Fletcher and others as his style evolved.
questions.forensicLinguistics: Computer analysis of Shakespeare's linguistic fingerprint

questions.question: The 'lost years' (1585-1592) mystery deepens because no contemporary records exist of Shakespeare's whereabouts. What Catholic family's tutor records mention a 'William Shakeshafte'?
questions.hint: This Lancashire family employed a tutor with a suspiciously similar name
questions.explanation: Alexander Houghton's will mentions 'William Shakeshafte', possibly Shakespeare working as a Catholic tutor during his mysterious lost years, explaining his deep knowledge of law and aristocratic life.
questions.historicalMystery: The Catholic connection to Shakespeare's missing years

questions.question: Anti-Stratfordian theories claim the real author was Christopher Marlowe. What specific linguistic evidence supports this, involving shared rare classical references?
questions.hint: Both writers showed identical knowledge of obscure classical texts
questions.explanation: Marlowe and Shakespeare share remarkably similar classical allusions and Latin quotations, particularly from Ovid's 'Metamorphoses', leading some to theorize they were the same person.
questions.marloweTheory: The linguistic evidence for hidden authorship

questions.question: Shakespeare's vocabulary is estimated at 15,000-29,000 words. What percentage of these words appear only once in his entire corpus, suggesting vast reading?
questions.hint: It's a surprisingly high percentage, indicating breadth rather than repetition
questions.explanation: About 40% of Shakespeare's vocabulary appears only once (hapax legomena), indicating either vast reading or access to specialized knowledge sources.
questions.vocabularyAnalysis: The statistical mystery of Shakespeare's word knowledge

questions.question: The phrase 'wild goose chase' first appears in 'Romeo and Juliet'. What was this originally - a real Renaissance activity?
questions.hint: It was an actual game played on horseback
questions.explanation: 'Wild goose chase' was a real Elizabethan equestrian game where riders followed a leader in formation like migrating geese. Shakespeare transformed the literal game into our metaphor for futile pursuit.
questions.literalToMetaphorical: How Shakespeare turned real activities into eternal metaphors
